questions.question: What is the central LLaVA projector choice for connecting a ViT to an LLM?
options: Insert gated cross-attention layers between every few frozen LLM blocks.
Project each ViT patch through a two-layer MLP into the LLM embedding space.
Compress all image patches into a fixed set of learned Q-Former queries.
Replace the ViT output with one supervised class label.
questions.explanation: LLaVA flattens each ViT patch and applies a two-layer MLP to map it into the LLM’s embedding dimension, then passes the projected patch tokens as visual context. Q-Former compresses them into learned queries; Flamingo inserts gated cross-attention instead.

questions.question: In LLaVA stage 1, which weights are trained on image-caption pairs with language-model loss?
options: The LLM only, while the ViT and projector remain frozen.
The ViT and LLM, while the projector remains frozen.
All three components, using image-classification labels.
Only the projector, while the ViT and LLM remain frozen.
questions.explanation: Stage 1 freezes the ViT and LLM and trains only the MLP projector using caption-conditioned language-model loss. Updating the LLM is part of stage 2 instruction tuning, not the initial alignment step.

questions.question: What data and objective define LLaVA's visual instruction tuning stage?
options: 1.2M class labels train the ViT with supervised classification loss.
158k GPT-4-generated visual-instruction turns train the projector and LLM.
558k image-caption pairs train only the projector with caption LM loss.
400M image-text pairs train both towers with contrastive loss.
questions.explanation: LLaVA stage 2 uses 158k GPT-4-generated visual-instruction turns and trains the projector with the LLM. The 558k image-caption pairs are stage 1 alignment data and train the projector while the backbones remain frozen.

questions.question: Before tokenization, what happens to the LLaVA <image> placeholder for a base image with 576 patches?
options: It is replaced by the 576 projected visual tokens.
It remains one literal text token and the patches are discarded.
It is replaced by one CLS token from the vision encoder.
It expands into 2880 tokens for every image resolution.
questions.explanation: The <image> marker is a placeholder that preprocessing replaces with the projected visual-token block before the LLM reads the prompt. With 576 base patches, the block contains 576 tokens; leaving the literal marker would discard image features.

questions.question: An AnyRes image uses a 2x4 grid of 336x336 crops plus one 336x336 thumbnail. If each crop yields 576 tokens, how many visual tokens are inserted?
options: 5,184 tokens, from (8 crops + 1 thumbnail)*576.
2,880 tokens, from 4 crops plus a thumbnail.
576 tokens, because the image has one global placeholder.
4,608 tokens, from 8 crops*576 without a thumbnail.
questions.explanation: Each of the eight AnyRes crops and the global thumbnail contributes 576 tokens, so (8+1)×576=5,184 visual tokens. The 4,608 option counts only the crops and omits the thumbnail; AnyRes includes that global overview alongside local tiles.

questions.question: A task values raw patch detail and has ample LLM context. Which bridge tradeoff favors LLaVA's projector over Q-Former?
options: The Q-Former sends all 576 patches and therefore preserves more raw tokens.
The MLP removes image tokens and relies on class labels instead.
The MLP sends every patch token to the LLM, preserving direct patch-level access.
The MLP compresses every image into 32 queries to save context.
questions.explanation: The MLP passes every projected patch token to the LLM, preserving spatial detail when context is available. Q-Former compresses the image to 32 queries, reducing context use but limiting direct access to each patch.
